feedback: If the paper coat soaked through: 'The paper let the rain through because it is absorbent — the coat's job is to keep rain out, so we need a waterproof material like plastic.'
If a child picks a material by looks: 'The shiny one looks nice, but what does the coat need to DO? Which material keeps the rain out?'

For the window trade-off: 'The metal kept the rain out but you couldn't see through it, and the cardboard went soggy and dark. Glass is transparent AND waterproof, so it does both jobs the window needs.'
Chocolate teapot (adult-run): 'It started to soften and melt when the warm water went in — chocolate melts when it gets warm, so it can't do a teapot's job.'
activities.intendedInsight: The right material rescues a job and the wrong one visibly lets it down, so a property is a REASON for a choice, not just a label; some jobs demand more than one property at once.
learnerActions: Pick an everyday object with a clear job — a rainy-day coat, an umbrella, a saucepan, a window, a boot.
Choose a material for it from a small set (e.g. paper, plastic, glass, cardboard, metal).
State out loud, before testing, which property you think matters and why you picked that material.

Observe or act out what happens when the object is used: pour water on the coat, let 'rain' hit the window. Any test involving heat (a saucepan near a hob, warm water on chocolate) is run by an adult as a demonstration, or acted out in pretend play — children do not hold materials near real heat.
Compare the result to your prediction: did the paper coat let the rain soak through? Did the plastic coat bead the drops off? Name the property that decided the outcome.
Watch the absurd choice (an adult pours warm water into a chocolate teapot) and describe what goes wrong and why.

For the window, compare glass (you can see out AND rain stays out) with a sheet of metal (rain stays out but it is dark — you cannot see through it), with cardboard (dark, and it goes soggy and lets water through), and with no material (wet) to discover that some jobs need TWO properties at once.
activities.title: Kit out the job: choose a material and see if it works

feedback: Raincoat, plastic vs paper: 'Plastic wins because it is waterproof; paper would fail because it is absorbent and would soak through.'
Glass hammer: 'A hammer needs to be hard and tough — glass is hard but brittle, so it would be likely to crack or shatter when it hit something.'
If a child names only one property for a boot: 'Good — it's waterproof. A boot also has to bend as you walk, so what else does the material need to be? (flexible).'
activities.intendedInsight: Judging two materials against each other for one purpose forces you to weigh a property against a need, which is stronger than judging a single material in isolation.
learnerActions: Take one job (a raincoat, a drinking cup, a hammer) and two candidate materials.
Decide which material is better for that job and SAY the property that makes it win.
Run the reasoning in reverse: explain why the other material would be a poor choice.
Sort a small set of materials into 'suitable' and 'unsuitable' for a named job, giving a property reason for each.
Spot the silly material in a set (e.g. a glass hammer among metal tools) and explain what would go wrong.
activities.title: Which is better for this job — and why? (head-to-head)

feedback: 'Macintosh needed something rain couldn't get through — he used rubberised fabric because it is waterproof.'
If the child says 'paper' for the coat: 'Would paper keep the rain out? Why not? What property do we need instead?'
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a material is a real human problem-solving act: an inventor matches a material's property to the job that needs doing.
learnerActions: Hear a short story of an inventor who solved a real problem with a material: Charles Macintosh and the waterproof coat, John Dunlop and the air-filled (pneumatic) rubber tyre, John McAdam and road surfacing made of layers of crushed stone.
Say what problem the inventor faced and which property of the material they chose solved it.
Take on a design brief in role — e.g. 'I need a coat that keeps the rain out' — choose a material and justify it, answering 'why not paper?' follow-up prompts.
Keep turns short; speak or act out the justification rather than writing long answers.
activities.title: The inventor's problem (material choice as problem-solving)
